newsitem.title: PERU: Defiant Peruvian guerrillas keep 140 hostages.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Peruvian guerrillas keep 140 hostages.

text.p: Defiant Marxist guerrillas held fast on Monday to 140 high-profile hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima after releasing 225 men the night before as a Christmas goodwill gesture.

Despite the mass release, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels showed no signs of giving into Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's demands that they lay down their arms and free the remaining captives.

A red-and-white Peruvian flag, decorated with a gun, a hammer, and the head of Tupac Amaru -- an Indian leader who led a 18th century uprising against Spanish conquerors -- hung provocatively from a window of the residence.
In a tumultuous scene late on Sunday, the released men filed out one-by-one to the cheers and applause of more than a thousand waiting relatives, journalists and officials.

Looking tired but elated to be out after five days of captivity, the men waved to cameras and made victory signs before being whisked away in five buses to a police hospital for routine medical checks.

Those released included the ambassadors of Bolivia, Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Venezuela and Cuba, as well as diplomats from Bolivia, the European Union, the United Nations, Britain, Spain, Germany and reportedly at least seven U.S. officials.
"Daddy, Daddy," shouted one young Asian girl on a man's shoulder as she finally recognised her father in one of the buses. Others wept or cried out in joy.

The releases brought a wave of joy throughout Peru, but this was tempered by concern for the remaining captives, who include some of Peru's leading government officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen and a handful of diplomats.
"I am here to thank God because he freed my brother last night, but I am staying until they all come out," said Enrique Selada, outside the residency with a lighted candle on Monday morning.

President Alberto Fujimori, himself the son of Japanese immigrants, greeted the freed captives in hospital, but left gravely without a word to reporters. His brother, Pedro Fujimori, was still being held hostage.

The guerrillas said they freed the non-government hostages as a "Christmas gesture." But a rebel statement warned the remaining captives would not be allowed out unless the government set free more than 400 of their jailed comrades.
Fujimori has flatly rejected this demand.
The statement also warned the government that "if Mr Fujimori decides on a military solution he will always find a Tupac Amaru member vigilant."
Fujimori told the rebels on Saturday he would rule out force provided they laid down arms and freed all hostages.
Crack Peruvian troops have drawn up a provisional plan to assault the residence, and U.S., British and German special units are in Lima to help if necessary, police sources said.
About 900 policemen surrounded the residency on Monday, the same number who have kept guard throughout the crisis.

Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig, whose men checked off the freed captives' names from a list, confirmed to reporters outside the residence that 225 were freed on Sunday night and said "just over" 140 remained inside under the guns of about 20 rebels.

"The worst thing really was the lack of any information, and not knowing from hour to hour what might be going on outside, what sort of negotiations might be being done," said released hostage Lucho Sakode, 47. "But we were all happy that our wives had been freed first and that at least they were okay. That kept me going."

The guerrillas released all women and elderly -- including Fujimori's mother and daughter -- hours after storming the residence during a plush cocktail party on Tuesday. Another 38 men were freed on Friday.

The newly-freed hostages filed out of the grand front entrance of the embassy just before 10 p.m. local time (0300 GMT on Monday) under the gaze of Red Cross officials. They still had on the suits they wore to the party.
Many carried small plastic bags, apparently with dirty underwear inside.
On their way to the police hospital, cars honked their horns in solidarity. Crowds lined the streets cheering and waving flags.

"We are proceeding to free people who are not connected to the policy of the regime directly or indirectly as a Christmas gesture," said the rebel statement that was read to waiting reporters by one of the first released hostages, former Peruvian labour minister Sandro Fuentes.
The statement angrily condemned Fujimori's tough stance and insisted that the MRTA was a champion of the marginalized masses in this impoverished Andean nation of 24 million.
Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, the ill-fated host of the cocktail party who has maintained morale inside throughout the crisis, remained inside his residence.
Others still inside included Latin American and Asian diplomats, about 40 Japanese businessmen and Peruvian officials, including two ministers and the head of Peru's anti-terrorism police.
The MRTA's assault is considered one of the most audacious and -- given the number and status of their captives -- most successful guerrilla actions in Latin America's strife-ridden history.
In Tokyo, Emperor Akihito cancelled celebrations for his birthday on Monday in solidarity with the remaining captives.
Sunday night's sudden and dramatic mass release came as a surprise after little sign of progress in negotiations.
The exit of the 225 men eased overcrowding at the residence, normally home to only six people. Water, electricity and phone services to the building remained disconnected on Monday.
The remaining hostages passed their sixth night on the floor inside the sweltering building.
"We had obviously been very cramped, and we were aware that they had to release a large number of hostages at a certain point," said freed Peruvian businessman Samuel Gleiser.
